title: An AI system is not just a single model
body: An AI system isn’t made up of just a single model. Actual services involve multiple stages, such as input preparation, searching, evidence selection, prompt generation, model invocation, output validation, log storage, and cost management. The model is merely the core component responsible for generating answers or making decisions. When reading code, don’t just look at the line that calls the model; to understand the overall structure, you must also examine what data is prepared beforehand and what validation is performed afterward. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving a problem, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. AI system code does not end with a single model call. It often involves a series of steps, including data collection, preprocessing, searching, prompt construction, model responses, post-validation, and log storage. When analyzing the structure, examine what inputs each step receives and what outputs it produces. It is also important to identify at which layer a problem occurred in the event of a failure.

title: Prompt: Instructions for the model
body: A prompt is a set of instructions given to the model. While it can consist solely of a user’s question, in actual services, it often includes the model’s role, response format, prohibited actions, reference materials, and examples. A good prompt clearly tells the model what it should and should not do. When reading code, if the prompt is a long string, it should be treated as a critical setting for adjusting output quality. In RAG, retrieved evidence can also be included in the prompt. A prompt is a set of instructions that informs the model of its role, input, output format, and constraints. When reading code, you should check whether only the user’s question is sent, or if system rules, examples, and search criteria are included as well.

title: Context Window: The range the model can see at one time
body: A context window is the amount of information a model can reference in one request. The limit is measured in tokens rather than characters, and system instructions, the user request, prior conversation, and retrieved documents all share that space. If the input is too large, an API may reject it or the application may need to remove content, leaving less room for the answer. Read long-document code by tracing ① how the document is chunked, ② which chunks are selected for the question, ③ whether instructions and evidence are prioritized, and ④ how the total token budget is checked.

detail: The context window is the maximum amount of input a model can process at one time. Since it cannot accommodate entire long documents or lengthy conversations, it is necessary to perform searches, summarization, chunk selection, and prioritization. When reading code, ensure that the prompt length, the number of search results, and the maximum token setting do not conflict with one another.

title: Chunking: Breaking Down Long Documents
body: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into smaller pieces. Since models and search systems have difficulty handling documents that are too long all at once, they split them into paragraphs or sections and store and search them in that format. In RAG, chunks relevant to the query are identified and passed to the model. If the chunks are too large, irrelevant content may be included; if they are too small, the context may be disrupted. When reading code, you should verify how chunk size, overlap, and source text location information are managed. title: Fine-tuning: Changing the Model's Behavior
body: Fine-tuning uses additional training data to adapt output format, tone, decision patterns, or task ability. It may teach some facts, but it is not a guaranteed way to retrieve current knowledge; changing facts are better handled with retrieval or tools. Check the train/evaluation split, base model, checkpoint, and model actually loaded for inference.

title: LoRA: How to Perform Lightweight Fine-Tuning
body: LoRA is a method for tailoring a large model to a specific format or task by training only a small set of additional weights, without having to retrain the entire model. Training the entire model is costly and time-consuming, but LoRA allows for relatively lightweight experimentation. However, LoRA does not provide all the necessary knowledge from scratch, so data quality and the target format are crucial. When reading code, think of LoRA as an adapter that is added on top of the base model. Typically, the base model remains unchanged, and only additional weights are applied to teach it a specific style or format. When reading the code, you should check the base model path, the adapter path, whether they are merged, and which files are loaded during inference.

title: Inference: The step of generating answers using the trained model
body: Inference is the process of using a trained model to generate actual answers or predictions. If training is the process of teaching the model, then inference is the process of feeding input into the trained model and receiving the results. When a chatbot answers a question or an image model classifies an image, that is also inference. When reading code, inference involves model loading, input preprocessing, prediction execution, and output postprocessing. Cost and latency also become important during the inference stage. Inference is the stage where a trained model is used to generate actual answers. When reading the code, you should verify the sequence of model loading, input preprocessing, generation options, and output postprocessing. Its purpose differs from that of the training code.

Even with the same model, response times can vary depending on the input length and generation options.

title: Latency: The time it takes to receive a response
body: Latency is the time it takes for a response to be returned after a request is sent. In AI apps, model calls, searches, database queries, and network round-trip times all affect latency. If the response takes too long, users may feel as though the service has stopped working. That’s why techniques such as caching, short inputs, fast searches, and streaming output are used. When reading code, you should check the sections related to latency for any repetitive calls or unnecessarily time-consuming operations. Latency is directly linked to the time a user spends waiting. When reading AI service code, you should break down the process to identify where most of the time is spent: during search, model invocation, post-processing, or network round-trip.

title: Hallucination: A Plausible Wrong Answer
body: Hallucination is fluent output that is unsupported or false. Retrieval, citations, validators, and abstention rules can reduce risk but do not guarantee accuracy. Verify that citations support the claims and use trusted tools or rules for consequential facts.

title: Guardrail: A Safety Mechanism for AI Outputs
body: Guardrail is a safety mechanism for AI outputs. Since models can generate incorrect, dangerous, or unformatted answers, services implement safeguards such as prohibition rules, output validation, justification checks, and handling of follow-up questions. For example, in a learning app, rules can be set to restrict terminology that exceeds a student’s level or to provide hints rather than immediately revealing the correct answer. When reading code, Guardrail connects to the validation logic before and after the model. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. This approach allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. A guardrail is a safety mechanism that prevents AI output from veering into dangerous or inaccurate directions. It may include rules such as blocking prohibited topics, requiring sources, removing personal information, and verifying formatting. When you encounter a guardrail while reading code, you should determine at which stage—before or after the model’s response—the check occurs, and whether it results in blocking, modification, or a warning.
